=====camden/PROMPTLOG.md=====
# PROMPTLOG — Camden Thomas

**6–10 annotated episodes by M5.** Required coverage (handout §12):

- [ ] One **revised plan** — a plan you rejected or changed, and why
- [ ] One **rejected diff** — code the agent produced that you did not merge, and what
      was wrong with it
- [ ] One **tool-output debugging loop with real hardware evidence** — dmesg, a timing
      capture, /proc/interrupts before and after
- [ ] One **review of your partner's work** — what you questioned, what the answer was,
      what changed

> Write these **as they happen**. A log reconstructed in Week 15 reads like a log
> reconstructed in Week 15, and one of these episodes is defended out loud on demo day.
>
> "A team whose two halves never disagreed about anything all semester has not been
> reviewing."

---

## Episode template

### E-00 — (short title)

**Milestone:** M?  **Date:**
**Category:** plan / rejected diff / hardware loop / partner review

**Context.** What I was trying to do and what I already knew.

**What I asked.** The actual prompt, or its substance. Include the evidence I pasted.

**What came back.** Summarized, with the part that mattered quoted.

**My judgment.** What I accepted, what I rejected, and *why* — this paragraph is the
one that is graded and the one I will be asked to defend.

**Outcome.** Commit(s), and what I would do differently.

---

## Episodes

### E-01 — The board that never populated

**Milestone:** M0  **Date:** 2026-09-11  **Category:** revised plan

> **DRAFT — evidence only.** Everything below the line in *What came back* is the record
> of what actually happened, assembled from the session transcript so the details are
> exact rather than remembered. **"My judgment" is deliberately empty: that paragraph is
> the graded one and the one I will be asked to defend out loud, so it has to be mine.**
> Rewrite the rest in my own voice and delete this note before committing.

**Context.** `tools/bootstrap_board.sh` was supposed to create the whole GitHub board —
7 labels, 7 milestones, ~80 issues and ~90 blocked-by dependencies — in one run. I ran it
dry, then for real, twice. Nothing appeared in Issues, nothing appeared on the project
board, and the script never seemed to finish. I had no error message to work from.

**What I asked.** To diagnose why the script produced nothing, and then to compare the
generate-once-from-a-script approach against a one-time setup that I adjust incrementally
as questions get answered — because what I actually need is for answers from Lance and me
to propagate into the board and the docs, not for the whole plan to be regenerated.

**What came back.** Five separate faults, found by running things rather than reading the
script:

1. **The script was never executed.** My shell history showed `./tools/bootstrap_board.sh`
   run from PowerShell. `bash` is not on PATH there, so PowerShell handed the `.sh` file to
   the Windows file association instead of running it — which is both why nothing happened
   and why it appeared to hang. The same script run under Git Bash produced correct
   dry-run output immediately.
2. **It never touched the project board at all.** Its own closing lines read
   `Next: 1. Add all issues to the project board and set up the columns.` Even a perfect
   run would have left the kanban empty.
3. **The token had no `project` scope.** `gh project list` returned
   `error: your authentication token is missing required scopes [read:project]`.
4. **`gh issue dependency` does not exist** in gh 2.100.0, despite the script's header
   claiming the feature "landed 2026-06". All ~90 dependency links would have silently
   degraded to plain comments, at two failed API round-trips each.
5. **Every failure was swallowed** — `2>/dev/null` on issue creation, `|| echo "(exists,
   skipping)"` on milestones, and a `set -e` bug on the final line that makes a *successful*
   real run exit 1. A half-broken run and a working run looked identical.

The deeper finding was architectural, and it is the one that mattered: the script was a
**generator**, not a **reconciler**. It refused to run a second time (`Open issues already
exist. Re-running would create duplicates.`), so it could not be used to add a single task
later, and the plan text lived in 33KB of bash that could not safely be re-executed. Fixing
the five bugs would have left that intact.

**What replaced it.** `docs/board.toml` as the source of truth, `tools/board_sync.py` as an
idempotent reconciler, `docs/board.lock.json` holding the slug→issue mapping. Verified by
running it three times: the first created 80 issues, the second reported
`created 0, updated 40`, the third reported `created 0, updated 0, reads 7, writes 0`.
Items absent from the manifest are never touched.

**My judgment.**

> *(Mine to write.)* The questions worth answering here:
>
> - I accepted the rewrite rather than the five bug fixes. Was that the right call, or was
>   it scope creep dressed up as architecture? What would I say to someone who argued the
>   script was two hours from working?
> - The diagnosis came from running `gh` commands and reading my own shell history, not
>   from reading the script. Four of the five faults were invisible in the source. What
>   does that say about how I should direct the agent when something "doesn't work"?
> - The agent's original `bootstrap_board.sh` asserted a `gh issue dependency` feature that
>   does not exist, with a confident version number and date. I did not check it. What is
>   my rule for that class of claim from here on?

**Outcome.** Commits: *(fill in)*. What I would do differently: *(fill in)*.

### E-02 — Avoid Overcomplicating CAN

**Milestone:** M1  **Date:** 2026-09-21  **Category:** plan change

**Context.**

**What I asked.** The actual prompt, or its substance. Include the evidence I pasted.

**What came back.** Summarized, with the part that mattered quoted.

**My judgment.** I had been digging around into ways to make accessing CAN simple for far
too long before even beginning the dreaded goal of untangling the car's CAN messages.

**Outcome.** Commit(s), and what I would do differently.

### E-03 — Which adapter, and does it work on a Mac?

**Milestone:** M2  **Date:** 2026-10-22 to 2026-10-26  **Category:** plan

> **DRAFT — evidence only,** written by the agent from the session, like E-01. Rewrite it
> in my own voice, write "My judgment" myself, and delete this note.

**Context.** Before buying the OBDLink LX (D-019), I wanted to log a drive from my Mac to
study the data before designing the pipeline around it.

**What I asked.** Whether the LX would connect to a Mac, since OBDLink lists only Android
and Windows, and whether a cheaper adapter was guaranteed to work on both the Mac and the
Pi.

**What came back.** The agent first said "yes" too confidently, then corrected itself:
the vendor list is a support statement, macOS normally exposes a Bluetooth SPP device as
`/dev/cu.*`, but no adapter is *guaranteed* on macOS, and it found no report of the LX
itself on a Mac. It recommended buying from a returnable seller and testing at the car.

**My judgment.** *(Mine to write.)* Was "likely, not guaranteed" enough to buy on? What is
my rule for an agent's first confident answer about hardware compatibility?

**Outcome.** Bought the LX. Tools and a run book for the first drive on branch
`camden/m2/car-ready-tools` (PR #155). The Mac pairing result goes in
`docs/hardware/first-drive.md`.

# Claude Code transcripts — Camden Thomas

Camden's raw `.jsonl` session files, copied out of Claude Code's own store. They are a
graded deliverable (handout §12, CLAUDE.md §9): **raw — not summarized, not exported, not
retyped, never edited.** Claude Code deletes its copies after `cleanupPeriodDays`, so this
folder is the only copy that is guaranteed to survive to Week 15.

## At the end of every session

Exit Claude Code first (`/exit`), so the session file is complete. Then, in a normal
terminal at the repository root:

### macOS: Camden's laptop (Ghostty, zsh)

On this Mac the repository is `~/dev/school/cs370/car-watch`, so Claude Code stores its
sessions in `~/.claude/projects/-Users-crash-dev-school-cs370-car-watch/`. The folder name
contains `car-watch`, not `CS370-Term-Project`, so use this pattern. Exit Claude Code
(`/exit`), open Ghostty, and paste this one line. It copies every session, stages them,
and shows what is staged:

```sh
cd ~/dev/school/cs370/car-watch && ls -d ~/.claude/projects/*car-watch*/ && cp ~/.claude/projects/*car-watch*/*.jsonl partners/camden/transcripts/ && git add partners/camden/transcripts/*.jsonl && git status --short partners/camden/transcripts/
```

The same thing, one step at a time, if you want to check the folder first:

```sh
cd ~/dev/school/cs370/car-watch
ls -d ~/.claude/projects/*car-watch*/
cp ~/.claude/projects/*car-watch*/*.jsonl partners/camden/transcripts/
git add partners/camden/transcripts/*.jsonl
git status --short partners/camden/transcripts/
```

The `ls -d` line must print exactly one folder, the one ending in `cs370-car-watch`. If
zsh answers `no matches found`, or prints a folder from another project, stop and list
`~/.claude/projects/` to find the right name before copying.

### Git Bash / Linux

```sh
cp ~/.claude/projects/*CS370-Term-Project*/*.jsonl partners/camden/transcripts/
git add partners/camden/transcripts/*.jsonl
```

### PowerShell

```powershell
Copy-Item "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\projects\*CS370-Term-Project*\*.jsonl" partners\camden\transcripts\
git add partners/camden/transcripts/*.jsonl
```

Then commit on the session's branch, so the transcripts ride that session's pull request:

```sh
git commit -m "M<n> process: copy out Camden's Claude Code transcripts"
```

Copying again is safe: a session file only ever grows, so a newer copy replaces an older,
shorter one of the same session.

**Match `*CS370-Term-Project*`, not `*CS370*`.** The wider pattern also matches the HW1
rbtree-lab project folder, and would copy another assignment's sessions into this one's
graded deliverable. Check what you are about to copy before you copy it:

```sh
ls -d ~/.claude/projects/*CS370-Term-Project*/
```

**If nothing is copied**, the project folder has a different name on this machine — list
`~/.claude/projects/` and use the folder whose name contains this repository's path.

# tools/ — Python is allowed here (and in its tests, `tests/tools/`) only

Per the handout: the systems core is C; the interface layer may use anything, but **no
graded mechanism may hide in it.** Nothing in this directory is part of the shipped
product's runtime path.

**Present:**

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `board_sync.py` | Mirrors the checklist in `docs/milestones.md` onto GitHub issues and the project board. Not a product tool at all — it is how the plan is maintained. See `docs/BOARD/BOARD.md`. |
| `pidscan.py` | Mode 01 supported-PID survey for one car: protocol, battery, VIN hash, one reading per PID. Feeds `pid-survey.md`, which sets each testbed's inputs (**D-022**). |
| `obdlog.py` | The drive logger: every supported PID to `data/drive-*.jsonl` (**D-033**), rpm and load one request in four (`--fast`), static PIDs once into the header, every answering ECU's line kept (**D-044**). Run book: `docs/hardware/first-drive.md`. |
| `obdsim.py` | The fake OBD2 port: an ELM327 emulator on a pty with a scripted drive (`--two-ecu` makes a second ECU answer some PIDs), for development and tests, never the soak's data source (**D-023**). Sessions against it are labeled `synth`. |
| `obdsum.py` | Per-session and per-PID summary of a drive log: rates, gaps, events. |
| `obdplot.py` | PNG figures of a drive log: every PID on one time axis, speed against rpm, reply intervals. |
| `obdview.py` | One offline HTML page per drive log to scrub, zoom and read every PID at once. |
| `obdbins.py` | Operating-point binning prototype: per rpm x load cell, each PID's mean and spread. A look at the data, not the product's analysis. |
| `obdlib.py`, `elm.py`, `macgps.py` | Shared code: reply parsing and PID decoding; one adapter session; optional Mac location. |
| `train/` | Model training (skeleton). Weights land in `models/` with the training commit in the header. |

**Planned — not written yet.** Listed so nobody looks for them:

| Tool | Purpose | Board item |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `replay.py` | Feed an `obdlog` capture through the real pipeline at its recorded timing, labeled `replay` (a `synth` capture stays `synth`). A legitimate systems artifact (handout §5). Today it is an M0 stub that exits 1. | `replay`, `replayjsonl` |
| `plot_soak.py` | RSS / CPU / event-count series from soak heartbeats → the figure docs/EVALUATION.md §3 requires. | `plots` |

**Setup:** `make toolcheck` builds `.venv/` from `requirements-analysis.txt` (pyserial,
matplotlib, numpy) and runs the tool tests in `tests/tools/` (D-032). Run a tool as
`PYTHONPATH=tools .venv/bin/python tools/<tool>.py`. Logging alone needs only
`requirements.txt`; `--gps` needs `requirements-gps.txt`.

**The labeling rule is absolute.** Every record and log line these tools produce carries
its `src`: `live` only for `obdlog.py` and `pidscan.py` talking to a real car, otherwise
`replay` or `synth`, all the way through to
the report and the demo screen.

# soak/ — the 48-hour key-cycle run

**What the soak is (D-023):** a 48-hour wall-clock window of the car's normal use. The box
boots at every key-on, records, and shuts down at every key-off, on the live car
(`src=live`). The fake OBD2 port (`obdsim`) is a development tool and is never the soak's
data source. The professor confirmed this reading (reported by Camden, 2026-10-26;
board item `profmail`).

The handout requires the logs to show, at minimum:

1. A timestamped startup.
2. A heartbeat **at least hourly** recording process liveness, resident memory (RSS),
   and cumulative event counts.
3. **At least one injected fault** during the run — physically unplug a sensor for ten
   minutes, or `kill -9` a sensor process — with detection, degradation, and recovery
   visible in the log.
4. An orderly state at the end.

Under D-023 these apply per session: every session logs its start, a heartbeat at start,
at least hourly while running and at its end, and says whether it ended in a clean
shutdown or was recovered at the next boot. The off periods between drives are deliberate
gaps between a logged shutdown and a logged boot.

Raw, unedited logs are the graded deliverable. **Do not tidy them.** Real systems are
never that tidy, and a cleaned soak log is the artifact this course is best equipped to
notice.

## Before the graded run

Start soak-style runs at small scale from **M3**, not M4: daily drives, plus overnight
bench runs on a home charger against `obdsim` (labeled `synth`) to find leaks. Every leak
found in Week 9 is a crisis avoided in Week 14. `make soakcheck` runs a one-hour bench
miniature.

Leave margin to run the graded soak **twice**. You will want to.

# carwatch — CS370 term project
# Systems core is C17 and must stay -Wall -Wextra -Werror clean (CLAUDE.md §2.4).

# CC is make's default, cc: gcc on the Pi and in CI, clang on macOS.

# The tool tests (tests/tools/, D-032) need Python 3.11 or newer, the version Raspberry Pi
# OS ships; the department machines put 3.9 on PATH as python3. Pick the first interpreter
# that is new enough; fall back to python3 so the error, if any, names the version.
PY       ?= $(shell for p in python3 python3.13 python3.12 python3.11; do \
              command -v $$p >/dev/null 2>&1 && \
              $$p -c 'import sys; sys.exit(sys.version_info < (3, 11))' >/dev/null 2>&1 && \
              { echo $$p; exit 0; }; \
            done; echo python3)
CSTD      = -std=c17
WARN      = -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wvla
OPT      ?= -O2 -g
CPPFLAGS += -Iinclude -D_GNU_SOURCE
CFLAGS   += $(CSTD) $(WARN) $(OPT)
LDLIBS   += -lm -lpthread

BUILD    = build
BIN      = $(BUILD)/bin

ALL_SRC    = $(wildcard src/*/*.c)
# Library objects: everything except the per-daemon entry points, which are main.c and,
# where one directory holds two programs, <name>_main.c.
COMMON_SRC = $(filter-out %/main.c %_main.c,$(ALL_SRC))
COMMON_OBJ = $(COMMON_SRC:%.c=$(BUILD)/%.o)

DAEMONS    = obdd storaged analyzed supervisor obdctl statusd
DAEMON_BIN = $(addprefix $(BIN)/,$(DAEMONS))

TEST_SRC   = $(wildcard tests/test_*.c)
TEST_BIN   = $(TEST_SRC:tests/%.c=$(BIN)/%)

.PHONY: all test asan memcheck soakcheck replay deploy clean boundary boardcheck \
        hwcheck hwdocs hwclean toolcheck run-status

all: $(DAEMON_BIN)

$(BIN)/obdd:       $(BUILD)/src/obd/main.o        $(COMMON_OBJ)
$(BIN)/storaged:   $(BUILD)/src/store/main.o      $(COMMON_OBJ)
$(BIN)/analyzed:   $(BUILD)/src/analysis/main.o   $(COMMON_OBJ)
$(BIN)/supervisor: $(BUILD)/src/supervisor/main.o $(COMMON_OBJ)
$(BIN)/obdctl:     $(BUILD)/src/interface/main.o  $(COMMON_OBJ)
$(BIN)/statusd:    $(BUILD)/src/interface/statusd_main.o $(COMMON_OBJ)

$(DAEMON_BIN):
	@mkdir -p $(BIN)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $^ $(LDLIBS)

$(BUILD)/%.o: %.c
	@mkdir -p $(dir $@)
	$(CC) $(CPPFLAGS) $(CFLAGS) -MMD -MP -c $< -o $@

$(BIN)/test_%: tests/test_%.c $(COMMON_OBJ)
	@mkdir -p $(BIN)
	$(CC) $(CPPFLAGS) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $^ $(LDLIBS)

# `all` first: every daemon must compile under the same flags as the tests, so `make asan`
# builds the daemons with the sanitizers too, not only the unit tests.
test: all $(TEST_BIN) boundary boardcheck toolcheck
	@fail=0; for t in $(TEST_BIN); do \
		printf '%-28s ' "$$(basename $$t)"; \
		if $$t; then echo PASS; else echo FAIL; fail=1; fi; done; \
	exit $$fail

# CLAUDE.md §2.1 — a grader must be able to confirm the boundary in sixty seconds (D-038).
# Network code only in src/interface/; Unix sockets only through src/ipc/uds.c. The
# check tests itself first: every case under tests/boundary/cases/bad_* must fail.
boundary:
	@tests/boundary/check.sh --selftest tests/boundary/cases
	@tests/boundary/check.sh . && echo "boundary                     PASS"

# docs/milestones.md is the board (D-020) - every task, question and decision
# in the project is a checkbox there. Validate it in the same gate as the C.
boardcheck:
	@$(PY) tools/test_board.py

# Python tool tests (stdlib unittest, tests/tools/). The venv is made on first use, and
# refreshed when a requirements file changes, so a fresh clone stays green; it needs the
# network for that install. Dev only (D-032).
.venv/.installed: tools/requirements.txt tools/requirements-analysis.txt
	@test -x .venv/bin/python || $(PY) -m venv .venv
	@.venv/bin/pip install -q -r tools/requirements-analysis.txt
	@touch $@

toolcheck: .venv/.installed
	@PYTHONPATH=tools .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests/tools -q && \
		echo "toolcheck                    PASS"

# Sanitized objects live in their own tree. Objects do not depend on the flags that built
# them, so sharing build/ let a plain `make` link against ASan objects and fail, and let
# `make test` rerun sanitized binaries without saying so.
# -fno-sanitize-recover makes a UBSan finding abort the test, so it cannot print PASS.
# LeakSanitizer is on by default on Linux (the Pi, CI); macOS arm64 does not have it.
asan:
	$(MAKE) BUILD=$(BUILD)/asan test \
	  OPT="-O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all -fno-omit-frame-pointer"

memcheck: $(TEST_BIN)
	@command -v valgrind >/dev/null 2>&1 || { \
		echo "valgrind not found: run make memcheck on the Pi or Linux (macOS has none)"; exit 1; }
	@for t in $(TEST_BIN); do valgrind --error-exitcode=1 --leak-check=full $$t || exit 1; done

soakcheck: all
	./soak/run_soak.sh --mini

replay: all
	@test -n "$(FIX)" || { echo "usage: make replay FIX=fixtures/<name>"; exit 1; }
	./tools/replay.py --fixture $(FIX) --label replay

# The phone page and API, on synthetic data, until it is wired to the real source (D-045).
# On the Pi, bind the access point's address: make run-status STATUS_ARGS="--bind 192.168.4.1"
STATUS_ARGS ?= --bind 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
run-status: $(BIN)/statusd
	$(BIN)/statusd $(STATUS_ARGS)

deploy: all
	@test -n "$(PI)" || { echo "usage: make deploy PI=pi@<host>"; exit 1; }
	@# Source only: no build trees, no Mac venv, no raw drive data or soak logs, no transcripts.
	rsync -a --exclude /build --exclude /.git --exclude /.venv --exclude /data \
	      --exclude /soak/logs --exclude /partners ./ $(PI):~/carwatch/
	ssh $(PI) 'cd ~/carwatch && make'

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- hardware
# KiCad 10. On Windows kicad-cli.exe is under
# "C:/Program Files/KiCad/10.0/bin/" and is NOT on PATH by default:
#   make hwcheck KICAD="/c/Program Files/KiCad/10.0/bin/kicad-cli.exe"
KICAD ?= kicad-cli
SCH    = electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.kicad_sch

# ERC as a build failure — the hardware equivalent of -Werror (CLAUDE.md 7.12).
hwcheck:
	@command -v $(KICAD) >/dev/null 2>&1 || { \
		echo "kicad-cli not found. Set KICAD=/path/to/kicad-cli"; exit 1; }
	$(KICAD) sch erc --exit-code-violations --format json \
	         -o electricalDrawing/erc.json $(SCH)
	@echo "erc                          PASS"

# Regenerate everything derived from the schematic. Never hand-edit the outputs.
hwdocs:
	@mkdir -p docs/figures
	$(KICAD) sch export svg --exclude-drawing-sheet -o docs/figures/ $(SCH)
	$(KICAD) sch export bom \
	         --fields "Reference,Value,Footprint,MPN,Datasheet,Qty" \
	         --group-by Value -o docs/hardware/bom.csv $(SCH)
	$(KICAD) sch export netlist -o electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.net $(SCH)
	@echo "Regenerated: schematic SVG, bom.csv, netlist."
	@echo "Commit the SVG — PRs touching hw must show a picture."

hwclean:
	rm -f electricalDrawing/erc.json electricalDrawing/drc.json

clean:
	rm -rf $(BUILD)

-include $(shell find $(BUILD) -name '*.d' 2>/dev/null)

content.content:
### 3.1 Two sensors that cooperate

Your device must incorporate **at least two physically distinct sensors**, and they must
**cooperate**: fused into one decision, correlated against each other, or feeding a single
shared pipeline whose behavior depends on both. Two independent demos stapled together at
the README do not satisfy this requirement. That's one sensor short of the assignment,
twice. Cooperation is also where the systems content hides. Two sensors almost never want
the same sampling rate, the same interface, or the same latency budget, and reconciling
those differences inside one program is the first real design problem this project hands
you.

### 3.2 Below the application layer: the mechanism menu

Your system must include **at least two** of the following mechanisms, implemented by you,
identified explicitly in your design document, and measured in your evaluation. This is the
guardrail that keeps the project an operating-systems project rather than a wiring
exercise.

| # | Mechanism | What "measured" means |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | A kernel module or character driver for one of your sensors, exposing it via `/dev` or sysfs | Correct concurrent access; behavior under load; a clean `dmesg` |
| **B** | Interrupt-driven input, with a head-to-head comparison against a polling design | Event latency distribution and CPU utilization, both ways |
| **C** | Real-time scheduling (`SCHED_FIFO`/`SCHED_RR`) for a latency-critical path | Jitter and deadline-miss rate vs. the default scheduler, under load |
| **D** | A custom storage layer: ring buffer, append-only log, or small FUSE filesystem, with an explicit crash-consistency story | Write batching and `fsync` discipline; recovery after a mid-write power cut |
| **E** | A multi-process architecture: sensors isolated in separate processes, a hub aggregating over IPC (shared memory, message queues, or Unix domain sockets), a supervisor that survives any child dying | Kill any child at any time; the system degrades, logs, recovers |
| **F** | A high-rate sampling pipeline with a no-drop guarantee: lock-free or single-producer/single-consumer ring between capture and consumption | Sustained rate with zero drops, proven by sequence accounting, under CPU contention |

Choose the two (or more) that **your problem demands**, not the two that look easiest. The
design document (Section 8) requires you to justify each choice from the user's
requirements, and the defense will test that justification. Figure 1 shows where these
mechanisms live in a reference architecture.

## 5. Building in an Imperfect World

Somewhere between the memo and the checkpoint, every team hits the same wall. It's worth
telling you now that **the wall is scheduled.** The sensor your design really wants is a
$400 thermal imager and your budget is $60. The $4 accelerometer you bought instead has a
noise floor sitting exactly where the interesting signal lives. The CO₂ sensor needs three
minutes to warm up and drifts with the weather. And the data you need at the scale you want
(a year of failing compressors, a winter of greenhouse nights, 104 labeled door events) does
not exist, can't be bought, and won't be gathered in one semester by one device on one
shelf. None of this means you chose the wrong project! It means the project has become real.
Engineering has been called the art of the possible. The phrase is not a consolation; it's
the job description. **The constraints are not in the way of the work. They are the medium
the work is done in.**

The unproductive response is to stare at what can't be done. The productive one is to ask,
repeatedly and in roughly this order, what can:

- **Substitute.** Downgrade the sensor; keep the problem. A PIR and a door switch see more
  of a household's rhythm than you'd guess a thermal camera was needed for. A microphone's
  RMS level is a serviceable occupancy proxy. And two cheap sensors that corroborate each
  other routinely outperform one expensive one standing alone. Notice that "corroborate each
  other" is Section 3.1 arriving early, wearing a budget. Record in the design document what
  you wanted, what you used, and what the substitution costs in capability.

- **Make your own ground truth.** You can't wait for the bearing to fail, so you provoke the
  conditions and label the recordings: the taped washer, the loosened bolt, the greenhouse
  vent propped open on purpose, a one-week paper logbook of real door events. **Ten labeled
  recordings you made are worth more than ten thousand unlabeled samples you found**,
  because you know what yours mean. And at the defense, you will be asked how you know.

- **Replay.** Build a harness that feeds recorded sensor streams through your real pipeline
  at real or accelerated speed. Now a month of "operation" fits in an afternoon, rare events
  can be rehearsed on demand, and regressions are caught by re-running last week. The
  harness is not a workaround to be embarrassed about. It's a legitimate systems artifact
  (real products are tested exactly this way), and building one that faithfully preserves
  inter-sample timing is engineering in its own right. **One rule, absolute: replayed or
  synthesized data is labeled as such everywhere it appears. In logs. In the report. In the
  demo. The 48-hour soak and the live demonstration run on live sensors; everything else may
  run on honest replay.**

- **Narrow the claim.** Shrink the sentence until it is true. *"Detects the three faults I
  can induce on this compressor, with these error rates"* is a claim that survives
  cross-examination; *"predicts failure"* is not. A narrow claim, met and measured,
  outscores a broad claim that's gestured at. On this rubric, and on every rubric that
  matters after this course.

What this means for your grade deserves to be said without hedging: **the term project does
not expect a perfect project. It expects an honest one that works.** We grade your reasoning
about constraints, never the absence of constraints, because the absence of constraints is
not a condition that occurs in nature. The design document has a home for this reasoning
(Section 8), and the evaluation report's limitations section is where it pays off. The team
that writes *"we wanted X, we could afford Y, and here is precisely what Y cost us"* has
demonstrated the exact judgment this course exists to build, and will be graded like it. The
team that quietly papers over the gap has converted an ordinary constraint (the most
ordinary thing in engineering) into an integrity problem. And that is the worst trade
available anywhere in this course. We live in an imperfect world. Every system you will ever
ship will ship into it. So you may as well learn to do it well, and without apology, now.

---

=====statusd_main.c 1-60=====
/* statusd: the phone page and API (D-013, D-043, D-045).
 *
 * A supervisable daemon (CLAUDE.md section 2.6): it exits 0 on SIGTERM or SIGINT, 1 when it
 * cannot run, 2 on bad arguments; it holds no descriptor but its listener (close-on-exec);
 * it logs a heartbeat at once and then every --heartbeat-s seconds; and nothing it does
 * depends on a sibling being alive, so a kill -9 of any other daemon changes nothing here.
 *
 * It serves only the box's own access-point address, never every interface: --bind has no
 * default but loopback. Until the real source exists it answers from the synthetic one,
 * and says so on every log line (src=synth).
 */
#include "common/log.h"
#include "interface/route.h"
#include "interface/server.h"
#include "interface/synth_source.h"

#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>

#define DEFAULT_BIND         "127.0.0.1"
#define DEFAULT_PORT         8080u
#define DEFAULT_HEARTBEAT_S  3600u
#define MAX_HEARTBEAT_S      86400u

typedef struct {
    const char *bind;
    uint16_t    port;
    unsigned    heartbeat_s;
} args_t;

typedef enum { ARGS_OK, ARGS_HELP, ARGS_USAGE } args_result_t;

static volatile sig_atomic_t g_stop;

static void on_signal(int sig)
{
    g_stop = sig;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ arguments */

static void usage(FILE *to)
{
    fprintf(to,
            "usage: statusd [--bind ADDR] [--port N] [--heartbeat-s N]\n"
            "  --bind ADDR       IPv4 address to serve on (default " DEFAULT_BIND ")\n"
            "  --port N          TCP port, 0 for any free one (default %u)\n"
            "  --heartbeat-s N   seconds between heartbeat log lines, 1 to %u (default %u)\n"
            "exit status: 0 stopped by SIGTERM or SIGINT, 1 could not run, 2 bad arguments\n",
            DEFAULT_PORT, MAX_HEARTBEAT_S, DEFAULT_HEARTBEAT_S);
}

/* s is wholly decimal digits and at most max. */
static bool parse_number(const char *s, unsigned long max, unsigned long *out)

####
# CI for the project board (CLAUDE.md 7.11, docs/BOARD/BOARD.md).
#
# Two guarantees, one workflow:
#   manifest - docs/milestones.md, the board, is well-formed (offline, always fast)
#   drift    - GitHub actually matches it, i.e. nobody forgot to run sync
#
# plus a third, soft for now: every PR traces back to an issue.
####
name: board

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: read

jobs:
  manifest:
    name: milestones.md is well-formed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: python tools/test_board.py

  drift:
    name: GitHub matches milestones.md
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      # --no-board keeps this inside GITHUB_TOKEN's reach: user-level Projects
      # need a PAT, issues do not. The board follows from the issues anyway.
      # --check exits 1 when anything would change.
      - name: board_sync --check
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: python tools/board_sync.py --check --no-board

  pr-closes-issue:
    name: PR traces back to an issue
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # SOFT LAUNCH. Failing red on your own PRs while you are still learning the
    # flow teaches you to bypass the check, which is the opposite of the point.
    # The 2026-09-26 target passed with the habit not yet set; delete this line when
    # the team decides it is (CLAUDE.md 7.5).
    continue-on-error: true
    steps:
      - name: body must contain "Closes #<n>"
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.pull_request.body }}
        run: |
          if printf '%s' "$BODY" | grep -Eiq '(close[sd]?|fix(e[sd])?|resolve[sd]?)[[:space:]]+#[0-9]+'; then
            echo "ok - PR closes an issue"
          else
            echo "::error::PR body has no 'Closes #<n>'. CLAUDE.md 7.5: every PR traces back to an issue; if there is no issue, add a line to docs/milestones.md and sync first (7.11)."
            exit 1
          fi=====provision_pi.sh=====

+/* Every descriptor the server makes is non-blocking and close-on-exec, so a poll loop

+static int nonblock_cloexec(int fd)

# Design document — carwatch

**User and problem.** Lance drives a 2015 CR-V daily, and nothing reads his engine's
sensors except a check-engine light that speaks only once something has failed. carwatch
is a box that boots at every key-on, records every Mode 01 sensor through a Bluetooth
OBD2 dongle, learns *this* car's normal, and flags behavior that leaves it before the
light would. It is also tested on Camden's 2008 Forester (D-022), which made the first
live capture on 2026-10-28 (`captures/forester/20261028T220659.957/`). **Claim (D-021):**
it learns the normal of the car it is installed in, flags behavior outside it and names
the likely fault area, with measured catch and false-alarm rates on faults we induce.

**Scope, cut 2026-10-28 with the TA's agreement.** The product is a Raspberry Pi 4 on the
owner's USB-C charger, an OBDLink LX dongle read over Bluetooth, and a phone page over
the box's own Wi-Fi. There is no sensor of our own, no battery, no supercapacitor and no
cooling: the engine's own sensors are the cooperating sensors, and every key-off is a
power cut. §7 says what that costs.

## 1. Architecture

```text
OBD2 port -- OBDLink LX (Bluetooth Classic SPP, D-019); the Forester speaks CAN 11-bit/500 k
   ~~ RFCOMM ~~> BlueZ -> /dev/rfcomm0 -> /dev/obd
  obdd       Mode 01, one request outstanding; measured 20.7 replies/s,
    |        request cycle p50 42 ms, p99 91 ms; rpm and load 2.6 Hz, each other PID 0.4 Hz
    | ring: SPSC in shared memory, 20.7 slots/s; refuse and count when full, never overwrite
    v
  storaged [D]  BEGIN..records..COMMIT, one fsync per second or 64 samples;
    ^           1.2 KB/s, about 4 MB per running hour -> 16 MB segments, ext4 on the SD card
    |           events from every daemon: one SEQPACKET Unix socket, a few per drive (D-042)
    | committed records only, read back from the log, about 1 s behind (D-031)
    v
  analyzed      bins -> baselines -> residuals -> trends -> model -> FSM; a few verdicts per drive
    v
  supervisor [E] fork/exec, heartbeats, restart with backoff --GPIO--> tri-color light (D-027)
    ^  Unix socket /run/carwatch/ctl.sock, on demand (D-043)
  obdctl (CLI)   statusd: GET-only HTTP over a poll() loop; page, JSON, CSV -> phone (D-013, D-045)
power: the owner's USB-C charger -> Pi 4. It dies at key-off, so every key-off is a power cut.
```

Every rate above is from the first Forester capture (54 s, 1113 samples, one ECU
answering, no `NO DATA`, no errors), made by the Python logger (D-033); `obdd` must match
it. One reply is one sample, one record and one analysis step. Queries go to the
supervisor, which asks the process holding the answer (D-043); `analyzed` never reads a
ring (D-031). `statusd` reads a *source* behind one function; today that source is
synthetic and every row it serves says `src=synth` (D-045), and the real one is a client
of the control socket.

## 2. Mechanism mapping

D and E are the committed pair (D-017). B and F stay declined: 21 samples a second never
stresses a ring, and there is no sensor of our own to drive by interrupt.

| Item | Component | Justification from the user's requirements | Measured by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D | `storaged`; checkpoints in `analyzed` | Power vanishes at every key-off and whenever the cable is pulled, yet the record and weeks of learned baselines must survive, and no baseline may learn a sample a cut later erased (D-031): append-only CRC'd records, 1 s commits, A/B checkpoints (D-025, D-035) | 50 cable pulls mid-write; records lost per cut; recovery time |
| E | `supervisor`, `src/ipc/` | A recorder that dies silently harms an owner who thinks it is on duty. Analysis, the least trusted code, must not take capture or storage down; the page server, the only network code, must not either | `kill -9` each child 20×: detection, recovery, fd leaks |

**Two distinct sensors that cooperate (handout §3.1).** The coolant thermistor, the
intake-air thermistor, the ambient-air sensor, the manifold pressure sensor, the mass
air-flow sensor and the oxygen sensors are separate transducers; the ECU only carries their
readings, and the dongle relays them. They want different rates (rpm and load every 0.4 s,
the rest every 2.6 s) and are reconciled in one pipeline: every sample is binned by the
rpm, load and coolant temperature current when it arrived, and every diagnostic in §3
fuses at least two of them. The TA agreed on 2026-10-28 that this satisfies §3.1 without
a sensor of our own. "Both sensors alive" (M2) is the committed live capture; "through the
pipeline" (M3) is the same sensors as committed records labeled `live`.

## 3. Analysis: how normal is learned and a fault area named

All our code (handout §3.3). Per committed sample, `analyzed` (1) bins by rpm × load ×
coolant temperature, so a cold idle is never compared with a warm cruise; (2) keeps per-bin
running mean and covariance (Welford), in A/B checkpoints; (3) scores the Mahalanobis
distance from the bin's baseline, which fires when a *partnership* breaks; (4) fits
Theil–Sen slopes of residuals across drives; (5) names the area with our classifier
(trained in `tools/train/`, inference in C; without weights, 1–4 still flag); (6) surfaces
verdicts through a hysteresis-and-dwell state machine.

The Forester publishes every sensor below (`hardware/pid-survey.md`); the CR-V is not yet
surveyed.

| Fault area (D-021) | Cooperating sensors (PIDs) | Signature | Induced by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cooling | coolant 05, intake air 0F, ambient 46, load 04, speed 0D | warm-up slope or settled temperature off its bin's normal for the same ambient and load | cardboard over the radiator |
| Air/fuel | fuel trims 06 and 07, MAP 0B, MAF 10, rpm 0C, O2 15 and lambda 24 | long-term trim rising at idle with idle MAP, shrinking with load | a small vacuum line opened |
| Sensor/electrical | the failed PID and its usual partners; module voltage 42; at a cold start, coolant, intake air and ambient | one PID absent or flat while its partners move; after a long soak, one temperature off the other two | a sensor unplugged |
| Unknown | all | residual high, no area matches | — |

No row can be called by one threshold on one value: each compares sensors that normally
move together, inside one bin. The first capture already shows the partnerships: at a warm
idle, coolant sat at 96–98 °C with intake air at 40 °C and ambient at 19 °C, and long-term
trim at −5 % against a 22 kPa manifold.

## 4. Failure-mode table

Log lines are `<process> <level> <event> key=value` with `src`; the table names the event.

| Component | Failure | Detection | Response | Log event |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| adapter | Bluetooth drops | `read` 0/`EIO`, `POLLHUP` | reopen `/dev/obd` with backoff | `link_lost`, `reconnected` |
| adapter | garbage or timeouts | parse failure; timeout | 3 in a row: `ATZ`, then reopen | `reply_bad`, `adapter_reset` |
| adapter | engine off, key in ACC | `0100` gets `NO DATA` | poll `0100` every few s, record nothing | `ecu_silent` |
| ECU | a sensor unplugged or failed | 5 `NO DATA` in a row; or pinned or flat while its partners move; MIL on (PID 01) | mark absent or suspect, retry each minute. ECUs often substitute a value and light the CEL: not caught before the light | `pid_absent`, `pid_flat`, `mil_on`, `pid_present` |
| any child | crash, `kill -9` | `waitpid` | restart with backoff; others run on | `child_exit`, `child_restart` |
| ring | consumer stalls | sequence gap; late heartbeat | refuse and count; restart `storaged`; red | `ring_full`, `heartbeat_late` |
| storaged | power cut mid-write (every key-off) | bad CRC or no `COMMIT` at boot | truncate the tail and the open batch (D-025) | `recovered` |
| storaged | disk full; `fsync` or write `EIO` | `ENOSPC`, return values | drop the oldest segment if allowed; hold the durable offset; degrade, red | `enospc`, `fsync_failed` |
| analyzed | torn checkpoint; bad model file | slot CRC; header CRC | other slot + redo; residuals only | `checkpoint_bad`, `model_unavailable` |
| `statusd` | a bad or oversized request; out of memory | the parser's limits; RSS | 4xx, 431 or 503; capture unaffected | `request_refused`, `report_failed` |
| supervisor | dies | systemd `Restart=always` | light freezes steady = "not running" | journal |
| clock | wall time untrusted at boot (no clock module, or its backup lost) | time before the build date | run on `mono_ns`; records carry `WALL_UNTRUSTED` | `rtc_invalid` |
| power | cable pulled, crank dip, or charger live at key-off | unclean end at the next boot; `vcgencmd` undervoltage; `0100` silent with power on | crash recovery (D); log; a silent ECU with power on is recorded, not a fault | `recovered`, `undervoltage`, `ecu_silent` |
| OS | power cut corrupts the root filesystem | boot fails | the root filesystem is read-only; only the log partition is written (board `rofs`) | journal |
| radio | Bluetooth and Wi-Fi share one chip | reply p99 in the heartbeat | measure (`btcoex`) | heartbeat |

## 5. Storage and data

- **Format (D-034, `include/store/record.h`):** a 40-byte header (`magic`, `kind`, `seq`,
  `mono_ns`, `wall_ns`, `src`, flags, `boot_id`), a typed body, a CRC32 over both. Kinds:
  sample, begin, commit, boot, shutdown, event. A sample is 56 bytes and keeps the reply's
  raw bytes beside the decoded value. 16 MB segments, never edited. A `src` of 0 is
  invalid and refused at the ring (D-040).
- **Rates, measured:** 20.7 samples/s is 1.2 KB/s, about 4 MB per running hour; a 32 GB
  card holds years of two-hour days.
- **Retention (D-041):** every segment is kept until the log filesystem is 80 % full, then
  whole segments go oldest first, never one the newest checkpoint still needs. Text logs
  go to the journal, size-capped.
- **fsync (D-035, `include/store/wal.h`):** commit at 1 s or 64 samples. A cut loses at
  most a second of signals that move over minutes; longer batches would lose warm-up at
  each cold-start reset; per-record `fsync` is 20× the flash wear. Measured in `expbatch`.
- **Crash story (coded, `src/store/wal.c`, tested across `kill -9`):** at boot `storaged`
  scans the newest segment, verifies CRCs, keeps everything up to the last `COMMIT`,
  truncates the rest (undo is truncation: nothing is overwritten), and writes a boot batch
  saying whether the last session ended clean. Since power dies at every key-off, almost
  every session ends unclean, and the soak measures recovery on every key cycle. `analyzed`
  loads the newest valid checkpoint and redoes later batches through the live code path
  (D-025).

## 6. The box: hardware and power

A Pi 4 with a 32 GB A2 microSD card, in a small shell with one USB-C port and one light;
the OBDLink LX in the car's OBD2 port; the owner's own USB-C charger and a short cable.
Nothing on the car is cut. Parts: `hardware/BOM.md`; connections: `hardware/wiring.md`.

Power is the charger's: live when the car runs, dead at key-off. The box therefore boots
unattended at every start and loses power at every stop. There is no stored energy and no
clean shutdown; mechanism D is designed for exactly that, and the root filesystem is
mounted read-only so a cut cannot corrupt the operating system (`rofs`). A clock module on
I2C keeps wall time while the box is off (`rtcspec`); without one, records carry
`WALL_UNTRUSTED` and time is monotonic only.

| State | Entered when | Supervisor does | Light (D-027) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `BOOTING` | power-on, about 30 s (`bootbudget`) | start children, await heartbeats | steady yellow |
| `RUNNING` | all healthy | record | green pulse |
| `DEGRADED` | child down, dongle silent with the engine on, storage fault | record what it can; log absent against crashed | red blink |
| `OFF` | power gone | nothing; the next boot recovers | dark |

## 7. Constraints and substitutions

| Wanted | Using | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every engine sensor | the 43 Mode 01 PIDs the Forester publishes (D-022); the CR-V not yet surveyed | oil pressure absent; lists differ by car |
| A sensor of our own beside the car's | none, since 2026-10-28 | the cold-soak cross-check uses the car's ambient sensor (46), which the car's own heat biases |
| A clean shutdown at key-off | none: power dies with the charger | the last ≤ 1 s of every drive is lost; the OS must tolerate cuts (`rofs`); every key-off is a recovery test |
| Failing engines | induced, reversible faults on two healthy cars (D-021) | a few fault areas; no real wear-out |
| Raw CAN at ECU rate | Bluetooth Mode 01 request/response (D-019): 20.7 replies/s, each slow PID every 2.6 s | no bus timing; a link that drops; most of the mechanism menu leaves the data path (D-017) |
| 48 continuous hours | 48 h of normal use across key cycles (D-023) | sessions with gaps; the professor confirmed this reading |
| Recording from key-on | a ~30 s Pi 4 boot (`bootbudget`) | the first half-minute of warm-up is lost |
| The product on the first drives | a Python logger, labeled `live` (D-033, D-046) | proves nothing about `obdd`; enters the product only as `replay` |

## 8. Evaluation plan

| Measurement | Method | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reply → durable, p50 / p99 | timestamps at tty read and after `fsync`; idle and with a CPU hog | ≤ 1.2 s / ≤ 2.5 s |
| Sustained request rate | answers per second from the log, per drive | ≥ 15/s (20.7 measured by the logger); rpm and load every ≤ 0.5 s, every other input every ≤ 3 s |
| `kill -9` each child | 20 trials per child, from the log | detect ≤ 100 ms; heartbeat ≤ 5 s; no fd leak |
| Ring drops under contention | sequence accounting | 0 |
| CPU per process | `utime` + `stime` in each heartbeat; idle and with a CPU hog | each daemon ≤ 10 % of one core; all ≤ 25 % |
| RSS over the soak | heartbeats at start, hourly, end, per session | slope < 100 KB per running hour |
| fsync batch size (`expbatch`) | per record, 1 s, 10 s on the Pi's SD: `fsync` p99, bytes written, loss per cut | 1 s: ≤ 1 s lost, ≤ ⅕ the bytes |
| Every failure-table row (§4) | inject each (EVALUATION.md §5) | its event logged; capture never stops for another's fault |
| Detection per fault area | 5 induced events per area | ≥ 4 of 5; ≤ 1 false verdict per 10 h |
| Recovery after a cut mid-write | pull the USB-C cable, 50 times, engine running | 50 / 50 recover; ≤ 1 batch lost |
| Key-cycle recovery (`keycyc`) | N real drives; unclean endings and records lost, from the boot records | every session recovered; ≤ 1 s lost each |
| Boot to first durable sample | log time against power-on | ≤ 45 s |

## 9. Ownership map

A subsystem belongs to whoever lands its first substantive commit (D-026).

| Subsystem | Owner | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/ipc/` ring and shared memory; `src/store/` record format, CRC32, write-ahead log and `storaged`; `src/common/` logging; build and `board_sync` | Camden | M0: 0e66851, 269e2c5; M3: 3860d8e, 9b145d4, aaac098, 972015a |
| `tools/` OBD2 logging and analysis tools; `scripts/capture.sh` and `captures/` | Camden | M2: PR #155, #183 |
| `src/interface/` HTTP parser, JSON, control-socket reply grammar, routes, `poll()` server, page and `statusd` | Lance | M3: 61be86f, 591718b, e316a32, 38c25ed (PR #184) |
| `src/obd/`, `src/analysis/`, `src/supervisor/`, `obdctl`, `tools/train/` | unclaimed | stubs only so far |

## 10. AI-use plan

Claude Code is used for planning, explaining kernel and serial mechanics, test fixtures,
tooling, adversarial review and drafting; never at runtime. A draft binds nothing until
one of us has read it: every choice Claude made without a human is named in the pull
request under "What I am least sure about" and in the `WHY` of the commit that made it
(CLAUDE.md §0, §7.7). The §3 fault-area rows and the §8 targets were drafted with Claude
and checked against the Forester capture; the transcripts are committed in `partners/`.
`src/` holds no network code except `statusd`, which serves the box's own access point
with no upstream (D-013, D-045); `make boundary`, in `make test`, fails the build
otherwise.

## 11. Changelog (M5)

What this M2 version got wrong, written at M5. Already known on 2026-10-28: the design of
2026-10-21 had a DS18B20 cabin probe with its own daemon, a supercapacitor power block
and a clean shutdown at key-off; all three were cut before any was built, and the code
still carries a second ring namespace reserved for the probe (board `probering`).

  raw bytes beside the decoded value. 16 MB segments, never edited. A `src` of 0 is
  invalid and refused at the ring (D-040).
- **Rates, measured:** 20.7 samples/s is 1.2 KB/s, about 4 MB per running hour; a 32 GB
  card holds years of two-hour days.
- **Retention (D-041):** every segment is kept until the log filesystem is 80 % full, then
  whole segments go oldest first, never one the newest checkpoint still needs. Text logs
  go to the journal, size-capped.
- **fsync (D-035, `include/store/wal.h`):** commit at 1 s or 64 samples. A cut loses at
  most a second of signals that move over minutes; longer batches would lose warm-up at
  each cold-start reset; per-record `fsync` is 20× the flash wear. Measured in `expbatch`.
- **Crash story (coded, `src/store/wal.c`, tested across `kill -9`):** at boot `storaged`
  scans the newest segment, verifies CRCs, keeps everything up to the last `COMMIT`,
  truncates the rest (undo is truncation: nothing is overwritten), and writes a boot batch
  saying whether the last session ended clean. Since power dies at every key-off, almost
  every session ends unclean, and the soak measures recovery on every key cycle. `analyzed`
  loads the newest valid checkpoint and redoes later batches through the live code path
  (D-025).

clean shutdown; mechanism D is designed for exactly that, and the root filesystem is
mounted read-only so a cut cannot corrupt the operating system (`rofs`). A clock module on

| `DEGRADED` | child down, dongle silent with the engine on, storage fault | record what it can; log absent against crashed | red blink |
| `OFF` | power gone | nothing; the next boot recovers | dark |

# Design document — carwatch

**User and problem.** Lance drives a 2015 CR-V daily, and nothing reads his engine's
sensors except a check-engine light that speaks only once something has failed. carwatch
is a box that boots at every key-on, records every Mode 01 sensor through a Bluetooth
OBD2 dongle, learns *this* car's normal, and flags behavior that leaves it before the
light would. It is also tested on Camden's 2008 Forester (D-022), which made the first
live capture on 2026-10-28 (`captures/forester/20261028T220659.957/`). **Claim (D-021):**
it learns the normal of the car it is installed in, flags behavior outside it and names
the likely fault area, with measured catch and false-alarm rates on faults we induce.

**Scope, cut 2026-10-28 with the TA's agreement.** The product is a Raspberry Pi 4 on the
owner's USB-C charger, an OBDLink LX dongle read over Bluetooth, and a phone page over
the box's own Wi-Fi. There is no sensor of our own, no battery, no supercapacitor and no
cooling: the engine's own sensors are the cooperating sensors, and every key-off is a
power cut. §7 says what that costs.

## 1. Architecture

```text
OBD2 port -- OBDLink LX (Bluetooth Classic SPP, D-019); the Forester speaks CAN 11-bit/500 k
   ~~ RFCOMM ~~> BlueZ -> /dev/rfcomm0 -> /dev/obd
  obdd       Mode 01, one request outstanding; measured 20.7 replies/s,
    |        request cycle p50 42 ms, p99 91 ms; rpm and load 2.6 Hz, each other PID 0.4 Hz
    | ring: SPSC in shared memory, 20.7 slots/s; refuse and count when full, never overwrite
    v
  storaged [D]  BEGIN..records..COMMIT, one fsync per second or 64 samples;
    ^           1.2 KB/s, about 4 MB per running hour -> 16 MB segments, ext4 on the SD card
    |           events from every daemon: one SEQPACKET Unix socket, a few per drive (D-042)
    | committed records only, read back from the log, about 1 s behind (D-031)
    v
  analyzed      bins -> baselines -> residuals -> trends -> model -> FSM; a few verdicts per drive
    v
  supervisor [E] fork/exec, heartbeats, restart with backoff --GPIO--> tri-color light (D-027)
    ^  Unix socket /run/carwatch/ctl.sock, on demand (D-043)
  obdctl (CLI)   statusd: GET-only HTTP over a poll() loop; page, JSON, CSV -> phone (D-013, D-045)
power: the owner's USB-C charger -> Pi 4. It dies at key-off, so every key-off is a power cut.
```

Every rate above is from the first Forester capture (54 s, 1113 samples, one ECU
answering, no `NO DATA`, no errors), made by the Python logger (D-033); `obdd` must match
it. One reply is one sample, one record and one analysis step. Queries go to the
supervisor, which asks the process holding the answer (D-043); `analyzed` never reads a
ring (D-031). `statusd` reads a *source* behind one function; today that source is
synthetic and every row it serves says `src=synth` (D-045), and the real one is a client
of the control socket.

## 2. Mechanism mapping

D and E are the committed pair (D-017). B and F stay declined: 21 samples a second never
stresses a ring, and there is no sensor of our own to drive by interrupt.

| Item | Component | Justification from the user's requirements | Measured by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D | `storaged`; checkpoints in `analyzed` | Power vanishes at every key-off and whenever the cable is pulled, yet the record and weeks of learned baselines must survive, and no baseline may learn a sample a cut later erased (D-031): append-only CRC'd records, 1 s commits, A/B checkpoints (D-025, D-035) | 50 cable pulls mid-write; records lost per cut; recovery time |
| E | `supervisor`, `src/ipc/` | A recorder that dies silently harms an owner who thinks it is on duty. Analysis, the least trusted code, must not take capture or storage down; the page server, the only network code, must not either | `kill -9` each child 20×: detection, recovery, fd leaks |

**Two distinct sensors that cooperate (handout §3.1).** The coolant thermistor, the
intake-air thermistor, the ambient-air sensor, the manifold pressure sensor, the mass
air-flow sensor and the oxygen sensors are separate transducers; the ECU only carries their
readings, and the dongle relays them. They want different rates (rpm and load every 0.4 s,
the rest every 2.6 s) and are reconciled in one pipeline: every sample is binned by the
rpm, load and coolant temperature current when it arrived, and every diagnostic in §3
fuses at least two of them. The TA agreed on 2026-10-28 that this satisfies §3.1 without
a sensor of our own. "Both sensors alive" (M2) is the committed live capture; "through the
pipeline" (M3) is the same sensors as committed records labeled `live`.

## 3. Analysis: how normal is learned and a fault area named

All our code (handout §3.3). Per committed sample, `analyzed` (1) bins by rpm × load ×
coolant temperature, so a cold idle is never compared with a warm cruise; (2) keeps per-bin
running mean and covariance (Welford), in A/B checkpoints; (3) scores the Mahalanobis
distance from the bin's baseline, which fires when a *partnership* breaks; (4) fits
Theil–Sen slopes of residuals across drives; (5) names the area with our classifier
(trained in `tools/train/`, inference in C; without weights, 1–4 still flag); (6) surfaces
verdicts through a hysteresis-and-dwell state machine.

The Forester publishes every sensor below (`hardware/pid-survey.md`); the CR-V is not yet
surveyed.

| Fault area (D-021) | Cooperating sensors (PIDs) | Signature | Induced by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cooling | coolant 05, intake air 0F, ambient 46, load 04, speed 0D | warm-up slope or settled temperature off its bin's normal for the same ambient and load | cardboard over the radiator |
| Air/fuel | fuel trims 06 and 07, MAP 0B, MAF 10, rpm 0C, O2 15 and lambda 24 | long-term trim rising at idle with idle MAP, shrinking with load | a small vacuum line opened |
| Sensor/electrical | the failed PID and its usual partners; module voltage 42; at a cold start, coolant, intake air and ambient | one PID absent or flat while its partners move; after a long soak, one temperature off the other two | a sensor unplugged |
| Unknown | all | residual high, no area matches | — |

No row can be called by one threshold on one value: each compares sensors that normally
move together, inside one bin. The first capture already shows the partnerships: at a warm
idle, coolant sat at 96–98 °C with intake air at 40 °C and ambient at 19 °C, and long-term
trim at −5 % against a 22 kPa manifold.

## 5. Storage and data
-- **Format (D-034):** 40-byte header (`magic`, `kind`, `seq`, `mono_ns`, `wall_ns`, `src`,
-  flags, `boot_id`), typed body, CRC32. Kinds: sample, begin, commit, boot, shutdown,
-  event; a 56-byte sample keeps raw reply bytes beside the value. 16 MB segments, never
-  edited.
-- **Rates:** 10–25 samples/s is 0.56–1.4 KB/s, 2–5 MB per running hour.
-- **Retention (D-041):** every segment is kept until the log filesystem is 80 % full,
-  then whole segments go oldest first, never one the newest checkpoint still needs. A
-  32 GB card holds years of two-hour days. Text logs go to the journal, size-capped.
-- **fsync (D-035):** commit at 1 s or 64 samples, and at clean shutdown. An unclean cut
-  loses at most a second of signals that move over minutes; longer batches lose warm-up
-  at each cold-start reset; per-record `fsync` is 20× the flash wear.
-- **Crash story:** at boot `storaged` scans from its last committed offset, verifies CRCs,
-  truncates the torn tail and any uncommitted batch (undo is truncation: nothing is
-  overwritten), and logs whether the last session ended clean. `analyzed` loads the newest
-  valid checkpoint and redoes later batches through the live code path (D-025).

# Wiring and electrical safety

The product is a Raspberry Pi 4 in a small box with one USB-C port and one light, plus a
Bluetooth OBD2 dongle in the car's OBD2 port (D-019). Nothing on the car is cut, spliced
or pierced, and nothing of ours is wired to it: the dongle plugs in, the box plugs into
the owner's charger. There is no power block, battery, supercapacitor, cooling or sensor
of our own (scope cut 2026-10-28, `CLAUDE.md` §3).

```text
  OBD2 port ──[OBDLink LX]~~ Bluetooth (RFCOMM) ~~▶ Pi (/dev/rfcomm0 → /dev/obd)

  owner's USB-C charger ──USB-C cable──▶ Pi 4 USB-C power input
  Pi GPIOs ──resistors──▶ tri-color LED ──▶ GND                     (the light, D-027)
  Pi I2C (GPIO2 SDA, GPIO3 SCL) ──▶ clock module, powered from 3.3 V (`rtcspec`)
```

> **The Pi's GPIO is 3.3 V and has no over-voltage protection.** Power every header
> part from the 3.3 V pin, never 5 V, and wire with the Pi powered off.

## OBD2 dongle → Pi (D-019)

| Item | Value | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dongle | OBDLink LX (STN chip; reports itself as `ELM327 v1.4b`) | **Bluetooth Classic, Serial Port Profile. Not BLE:** a BLE-only adapter has no RFCOMM channel and will not bind. |
| Connection | The Pi's built-in Bluetooth | Paired and trusted once with `bluetoothctl`; record the dongle's MAC address here when the Pi is paired (`bench`). |
| Stable name | `/dev/obd` | `rfcomm bind 0 <MAC> 1` creates `/dev/rfcomm0` at every boot, and a udev rule links it to `/dev/obd` (`scripts/provision_pi.sh`). The daemon never opens an `rfcomm` number. |
| Baud | ignored | RFCOMM carries bytes without a line rate; `screen` and `obdd` may set any baud. |
| Protocol | `ATSP0` (automatic) | The dongle negotiated `ISO 15765-4 (CAN 11/500)` on the Forester (`pid-survey.md`). |
| Dongle power | OBD2 pin 16 — **live with the key off** | The dongle draws from the car even when parked. Measure its key-off current (`dongledrain`) before leaving it plugged in overnight. |
| On a Mac | `/dev/cu.OBDLinkLX` | Pairs from System Settings. Closing the port drops the link and reopening it gets no bytes (2026-10-28), so the adapter is opened once per run (`scripts/capture.sh`). |

## Power: the owner's charger

The Pi takes whatever USB-C charger the owner has. It is live when the car runs and
dead at key-off, so the box boots at every start and loses power at every stop; the
storage layer recovers the log at the next boot (`DESIGN.md` §5, §6). Two things to
prove with a meter, not assume:

| Measurement | How | Feeds | Date | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Does the owner's charger go dead with the key off? Is it live in accessory? | USB-C meter, key off / ACC / run | `keyoff` | | |
| Does the supply dip at crank reboot the Pi? | watch the light at a cold start | `keyoff` | | |
| `vcgencmd get_throttled` after a cold start | on the Pi; must be `0x0` | `keyoff` | | |
| Boot time on the real image | `systemd-analyze`, log timestamps | `bootbudget` | | |
| Dongle key-off current from pin 16 | meter | `dongledrain` | | |

A charger that stays live with the key off keeps the box on; it then sees a silent ECU
and records nothing (`ecu_silent`). An undervolted Pi keeps running and corrupts the SD
card later: prove the supply, do not trust its label.

## The light → Pi (D-027)

One tri-color LED, written only by the supervisor. Two or three GPIOs, depending on
whether the part has its own yellow die or mixes red and green (`ledspec`). Each GPIO
drives its color through a resistor sized from the LED's datasheet, keeping the current
well inside the pin's limit. A pull holds yellow on from power-up, while the GPIO is still
an input, so a booting box shows steady yellow. Every live state is a pulse or blink; a
**steady** light, other than yellow while booting, or a dark one while the car runs, means
the device is not running.

## Clock → Pi (`rtcspec`)

| Clock pin | Pi pin | Pi signal | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SDA | 3 | GPIO2 (I2C1 SDA) | |
| SCL | 5 | GPIO3 (I2C1 SCL) | |
| VCC | 1 | 3.3 V | Power it from 3.3 V, so its I2C pull-ups never put 5 V on the Pi. Meter it before connecting. |
| GND | 6 | GND | |

The part and its backup cell or capacitor, and that backup's temperature rating, are
chosen in `rtcspec`. Without a clock the box runs on monotonic time and marks every
record's wall time untrusted (`DESIGN.md` §4).

## Bring-up order

1. Pi on the bench, dongle powered, no car: `bluetoothctl` pairs and trusts it, then
   `rfcomm bind 0 <MAC> 1`, `ls -l /dev/obd`, and `ATZ` answers with the dongle's
   version string. Reboot once and confirm `/dev/obd` comes back without a hand (`bench`).
2. Car, key to run, engine off: `0100` returns the supported-PID bitmap.
3. Car, engine running: `010C` (RPM) changes when you touch the throttle. Done on
   2026-10-28 from a Mac: `captures/forester/20261028T220659.957/`.
4. The charger measurements above, with the meter, at the next drive.

Measured results go in this file, dated. A step without a recorded result has not been
done (`CLAUDE.md` §8.4).

# Bill of materials

> **The OBDLink LX is bought** (Camden's PROMPTLOG, E-03) and both partners own a Pi 4.
> Everything else here is small and ordered only when its board line says so.

The product is a Raspberry Pi 4 in a small box with one USB-C port and one light, plus a
Bluetooth OBD2 dongle in the car's OBD2 port (D-019). The owner supplies the USB-C
charger. No power block, battery, supercapacitor, cooling or sensor of our own (scope cut
2026-10-28, `CLAUDE.md` §3).

## Core

| Qty | Part | ~Cost | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Raspberry Pi 4 (2 GB+) | owned | Both partners already have one. |
| 2 | 32 GB A2 microSD | $20 | A2 endurance matters for a key-cycle soak. Two, because the soak eats cards. |
| 1 | OBDLink LX, Bluetooth Classic OBD2 dongle (STN chip) | bought | The data path (D-019). Bluetooth Classic (SPP), **not BLE**. A cheap ELM327 Bluetooth clone is enough for a PID survey but is unreliable for a 48 h run. |
| 1 | USB-C cable, short, 3 A-rated | $6 | From the owner's charger to the Pi. |
| — | USB-C car charger | owner's | Not supplied: the box takes whatever the owner has. It must go dead with the key off (`keyoff`). |
| 1 | USB-C power meter (inline) | $10 | Settles "does this charger go dead at key-off, what does it deliver, and does it sag at crank" in seconds. |

**Fallback, not ordered:** a USB OBD2 adapter with an STN chip (e.g. OBDLink SX, ~$30,
D-015) if Bluetooth proves unreliable in the car.

## Small parts on the Pi's header

A part number is added only with its datasheet linked and checked by a human
(`CLAUDE.md` §8.4).

| Qty | Function | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Tri-color LED (red, yellow, green) + its resistors + the boot-time pull | The light (D-027). Two or three GPIOs, depending on the part; resistor values from its datasheet (`ledspec`). |
| 1 | Clock module on I2C, with its own backup cell or capacitor | Keeps wall time while the box is off. The backup's temperature rating must cover the cabin (`rtcspec`). |
| 1 | Shell: heat-resistant plastic (ABS, ASA or similar), vent slots, no metal near the antenna | `enclspec`. PLA softens near 60 °C, below a parked cabin's temperature. A food container is an acceptable prototype (handout). |

## Stretch — raw CAN (D-019)

Not ordered unless the stretch goal is taken up after mechanisms D and E are measured.

| Qty | Part | ~Cost | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | MCP2515 + TJA1050 CAN module | $8 | Check the crystal (8 vs 16 MHz) and meter MISO for 5 V before it touches the Pi. |
| 1 | OBD2 pass-through Y-splitter | $10 | Pins 6, 14, 5. |
| 1 | Logic analyzer (8ch clone) | $12 | Settles SPI timing arguments. |

# Supported-PID survey

**Sets the model's input list (D-021, D-022). Run it on each car's first drive.**

Method: `tools/pidscan.py`, as `docs/hardware/first-drive.md` describes (Mac or Pi). It
sends `ATZ`, `ATE0`, `ATSP0`, then the supported-PID bitmaps `0100`, `0120`, `0140`, ...
(each a 32-bit map of which PIDs in the next block the ECU answers), takes one reading of
every supported PID, and writes a markdown block that `scripts/capture.sh` commits beside
the drive under `captures/<car>/<time>/pidscan.md` (D-046). By hand, the same commands
work in `screen /dev/obd`.

## The cars

| | 2008 Subaru Forester (Camden) | 2015 Honda CR-V EX-L (Lance) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surveyed | 2026-10-28, parked at a warm idle, from a Mac | not yet (`pidhonda`) |
| Protocol (`ATDP`) | `ISO 15765-4 (CAN 11/500)` | |
| Battery (`ATRV`) | 14.0 V, engine running | |
| VIN | hash `16d15766b381`; model year 2008 from the VIN | |
| Supported Mode 01 PIDs | 43 | |
| Raw replies | `captures/forester/20261028T220659.957/pidscan.md` | |

The VIN is stored only as its hash (D-033); whether the raw VIN is also recorded is open
(`vinsurvey`).

## The sensors the design uses

A check mark is a live reading from the survey; the value is what the car reported at the
time, for scale, not a baseline.

| PID | Signal | Forester | CR-V | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0x01 | Monitor status: MIL and DTC count | ✓ `00 07 E5 00`, MIL off | | the failure table's `mil_on` |
| 0x0C | RPM | ✓ 649 rpm | | bin axis; polled at 2.6 Hz |
| 0x04 | Calculated load | ✓ 27 % | | bin axis; polled at 2.6 Hz |
| 0x05 | Coolant temp | ✓ 71 °C | | bin axis; cooling; cold-soak check |
| 0x0F | Intake air temp | ✓ 28 °C | | cold-soak check |
| 0x46 | Ambient air temp | ✓ 13 °C | | cooling; cold-soak check |
| 0x0D | Vehicle speed | ✓ 0 km/h | | cooling |
| 0x0B | MAP | ✓ 26 kPa | | air/fuel |
| 0x10 | MAF | ✓ 2.5 g/s | | air/fuel; both MAP and MAF are published |
| 0x11 | Throttle position | ✓ 15 % | | |
| 0x06 | Short-term fuel trim B1 | ✓ −1.6 % | | air/fuel |
| 0x07 | Long-term fuel trim B1 | ✓ 0.8 % | | air/fuel |
| 0x14–0x1B | O2 sensor voltages | 0x15 only, 0.84 V | | air/fuel; the upstream sensor is wideband, 0x24 |
| 0x24 | O2 sensor 1 lambda (wideband) | ✓ 1.00 | | air/fuel |
| 0x42 | Control module voltage | ✓ 14.0 V | | sensor/electrical |
| 0x5C | Engine oil temp | absent | | |
| — | Oil pressure | absent | | Not a standard PID. Nothing depends on it (D-021). |
| 0x2F | Fuel level | ✓ 34 % | | |
| 0x31 | Distance since codes cleared | ✓ 8309 km | | odometer proxy |
| 0x33 | Barometric pressure | ✓ 84 kPa | | matches Fort Collins' altitude; an altitude input for the bins |

The Forester also publishes 0x03, 0x0E, 0x13, 0x1C, 0x1F, 0x21, 0x2C, 0x2D, 0x2E, 0x30,
0x32, 0x34, 0x3C, 0x41, 0x43, 0x44, 0x45, 0x47, 0x49, 0x4A, 0x4C, 0x4D, 0x4E, 0x51 and
0x5A; the logger records all of them, decoded where `tools/obdlib.py` knows the formula.

## After the survey

Every supported PID becomes an input to the model for that car. Manufacturer (Mode 22)
PIDs are a stretch: try them only if a fault area has too few sensors to call.

# Supported-PID survey

**Sets the model's input list (D-021, D-022). Run it on each car's first drive.**

Method: `tools/pidscan.py`, as `docs/hardware/first-drive.md` describes (Mac or Pi). It
sends `ATZ`, `ATE0`, `ATSP0`, then the supported-PID bitmaps `0100`, `0120`, `0140`, ...
(each a 32-bit map of which PIDs in the next block the ECU answers), takes one reading of
every supported PID, and writes a markdown block that `scripts/capture.sh` commits beside
the drive under `captures/<car>/<time>/pidscan.md` (D-046). By hand, the same commands
work in `screen /dev/obd`.

## The cars

| | 2008 Subaru Forester (Camden) | 2015 Honda CR-V EX-L (Lance) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surveyed | 2026-10-28, parked at a warm idle, from a Mac | not yet (`pidhonda`) |
| Protocol (`ATDP`) | `ISO 15765-4 (CAN 11/500)` | |
| Battery (`ATRV`) | 14.0 V, engine running | |
| VIN | hash `16d15766b381`; model year 2008 from the VIN | |
| Supported Mode 01 PIDs | 43 | |
| Raw replies | `captures/forester/20261028T220659.957/pidscan.md` | |

The VIN is stored only as its hash (D-033); whether the raw VIN is also recorded is open
(`vinsurvey`).

## The sensors the design uses

A check mark is a live reading from the survey; the value is what the car reported at the
time, for scale, not a baseline.

| PID | Signal | Forester | CR-V | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0x01 | Monitor status: MIL and DTC count | ✓ `00 07 E5 00`, MIL off | | the failure table's `mil_on` |
| 0x0C | RPM | ✓ 649 rpm | | bin axis; polled at 2.6 Hz |
| 0x04 | Calculated load | ✓ 27 % | | bin axis; polled at 2.6 Hz |
| 0x05 | Coolant temp | ✓ 71 °C | | bin axis; cooling; cold-soak check |
| 0x0F | Intake air temp | ✓ 28 °C | | cold-soak check |
| 0x46 | Ambient air temp | ✓ 13 °C | | cooling; cold-soak check |
| 0x0D | Vehicle speed | ✓ 0 km/h | | cooling |
| 0x0B | MAP | ✓ 26 kPa | | air/fuel |
| 0x10 | MAF | ✓ 2.5 g/s | | air/fuel; both MAP and MAF are published |
| 0x11 | Throttle position | ✓ 15 % | | |
| 0x06 | Short-term fuel trim B1 | ✓ −1.6 % | | air/fuel |
| 0x07 | Long-term fuel trim B1 | ✓ 0.8 % | | air/fuel |
| 0x14–0x1B | O2 sensor voltages | 0x15 only, 0.84 V | | air/fuel; the upstream sensor is wideband, 0x24 |
| 0x24 | O2 sensor 1 lambda (wideband) | ✓ 1.00 | | air/fuel |
| 0x42 | Control module voltage | ✓ 14.0 V | | sensor/electrical |
| 0x5C | Engine oil temp | absent | | |
| — | Oil pressure | absent | | Not a standard PID. Nothing depends on it (D-021). |
| 0x2F | Fuel level | ✓ 34 % | | |
| 0x31 | Distance since codes cleared | ✓ 8309 km | | odometer proxy |
| 0x33 | Barometric pressure | ✓ 84 kPa | | matches Fort Collins' altitude; an altitude input for the bins |

The Forester also publishes 0x03, 0x0E, 0x13, 0x1C, 0x1F, 0x21, 0x2C, 0x2D, 0x2E, 0x30,
0x32, 0x34, 0x3C, 0x41, 0x43, 0x44, 0x45, 0x47, 0x49, 0x4A, 0x4C, 0x4D, 0x4E, 0x51 and
0x5A; the logger records all of them, decoded where `tools/obdlib.py` knows the formula.

## After the survey

Every supported PID becomes an input to the model for that car. Manufacturer (Mode 22)
PIDs are a stretch: try them only if a fault area has too few sensors to call.

### E-04 — The adapter that answered once

**Milestone:** M2  **Date:** 2026-10-28  **Category:** hardware loop

> **DRAFT — evidence only,** written by the agent from the session and the commits, like
> E-01. Rewrite it in my own voice, write "My judgment" myself, and delete this note.

**Context.** The first drive of the Forester, with `scripts/capture.sh` recording the
video clip for the M2 zip. The script ran `pidscan` (survey) and then `obdlog` (the drive
log) against the same Bluetooth serial port, as the run book said, and both had worked
back to back against `obdsim`.

**What I asked.** Why the survey printed 43 PIDs and then the logger sat at zero samples
on the same port, seconds later, engine running.

**What came back.** The evidence was the logger's own status line (0 samples, no error)
against the survey that had just succeeded, and `ls /dev/cu.*` still listing the port.
The agent's reading: on macOS, closing a Bluetooth SPP serial port drops the RFCOMM
link, and reopening the device node does not re-establish it, so the second process gets
a port that accepts writes and never answers. It is recorded in the script itself:

> On macOS, closing a Bluetooth serial port drops the link, and reopening the port does
> not bring it back: obdlog then gets no bytes at all (2026-10-28, OBDLink LX).

The fix (`b1a6819`): open a real adapter once per run. The logger owns the port, and
step 1 shows the newest live survey from disk instead of re-running `pidscan`. The next
run logged 1042 samples in 50.9 s (ended by Ctrl-C), and the one after it, 1113 samples
in 53.8 s at 20.7 samples/s, is the capture committed as `02ba151`.

**My judgment.** *(Mine to write.)* The simulator never showed this because a pty does
not have a link to drop. What is my rule for "it works on the simulator" from here on?

**Outcome.** Commits `b1a6819`, `02ba151`; `captures/forester/20261028T220659.957/`.
Open: whether the Pi's RFCOMM behaves the same way (`bench`).
EOF
